rows: 988 kg/m³: the neat polymer's 1040 kg/m³ less 5 % porosity; Fibre is denser than any matrix here, so a filled compound cannot be lighter than its polymer except by porosity (filament and printed-part densities sit a few percent below the resin's), nor heavier than the rule of mixtures at the most fibre a printable filament carries: 1/rho = (1 - w)/rho_polymer + w/rho_fibre.

1353 kg/m³: the rule of mixtures at 35 wt% glass-fibre; Fibre is denser than any matrix here, so a filled compound cannot be lighter than its polymer except by porosity (filament and printed-part densities sit a few percent below the resin's), nor heavier than the rule of mixtures at the most fibre a printable filament carries: 1/rho = (1 - w)/rho_polymer + w/rho_fibre.

polymer.basis: Classification and typical values from polymer handbooks and resin data sheets, as compiled for the estimate model (docs/audits/2026-09-15-filtering-estimates-data/physics/). The document cited prints a density inside the range, not its ends. DuPont's Zytel guide (R-DUPONT-ZYTEL-GUIDE) prints, for the unreinforced PA612 grades Zytel 151L and 153HSL, a density of 1060 kg/m³ (ISO 1183), a melting temperature of 218 °C (ISO 11357-1/-3) and a water absorption, similar to ISO 62, of 1.3 % at equilibrium at 50 % RH and 23 °C and 3 % saturated, immersed at 23 °C, p. 8.

Water or aqueous solutions at high temperature

All polyamides take up water when kept in a moist environment... Irreversible chemical damage to the material can only be caused by water or aqueous solutions at high temperatures. This is referred to as hydrolysis.
